analysis.one_liner: Requires private health insurance to cover prostate cancer screenings for high-risk men at no out-of-pocket cost.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the preventive-care coverage rules (the same part of law created by the Affordable Care Act) to require private health plans to pay the full cost of prostate cancer screening for men at high risk — African-American men and men with a father or brother who had prostate cancer — starting at age 40, even when federal screening guidelines don't call for it for the general population. The bill never got a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Men at high risk of prostate cancer — African-American men and men with a father, brother, or affected first-degree relative — would get PSA and other prostate cancer screenings starting at age 40 with no copay, deductible, or coinsurance, catching the disease early when survival is near 100% instead of 30% at late stage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Black men and men with family prostate cancer history

how_it_helps.text: Requires private plans to cover prostate cancer screenings for high-risk men — African-American men and men with a family history — with no copays, deductibles, or coinsurance.
Applies to men age 40 and over at high risk, even when the screenings fall outside what the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends for the general population.
Cites that early-stage prostate cancer has a near-100% survival rate versus 30% for late-stage, and that eliminating cost barriers helps catch the disease before it spreads.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and issuers, who would have to cover these screenings at no cost-sharing; the cost would ultimately be spread across premiums paid by all enrollees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, and ultimately all premium payers

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to private group and individual plans, so the cost of the added free screenings is folded into premiums paid by all enrollees rather than borne publicly.

Wider PSA screening can produce false positives and lead to unnecessary biopsies and treatment of slow-growing cancers that would never have caused harm — a tradeoff the USPSTF has historically weighed when limiting its own recommendations, which is why this bill adds coverage only for men at high risk.
The bill also codifies that the Task Force's current breast cancer screening recommendations govern, overriding its 2009 recommendations, a provision not central to the bill's stated purpose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a free, potentially lifesaving test for men at elevated risk, and catching prostate cancer early is far cheaper than treating it late. The costs are modestly higher insurance premiums spread across all policyholders and a marginally higher rate of false-positive diagnoses that can lead to unnecessary biopsies. On balance it is a low-cost, well-targeted preventive health mandate, though its value depends on screening actually improving survival for the groups covered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on introduction, and neither ever voted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 28, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 7, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which took no further action on it.
No version of the bill ever reached the House floor or the Senate; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers avoid the added mandate to cover free prostate cancer screenings for high-risk men; men at high risk forgo the no-cost benefit this bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers spared a new screening mandate

for.name: Rep. Larry Bucshon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the 118th Congress.

for.name: Reps. Yvette Clarke, Neal Dunn, and Troy Carter
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration in committee or subcommittee, leaving it without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan and lopsided: 74 of 216 House Democrats and 18 of 224 House Republicans signed on, but that support never translated into committee action.

industries.note: Insurers must now pay for free prostate cancer screening for high-risk men, adding to covered benefits; preventive screening is generally inexpensive relative to the late-stage cancer treatment they would otherwise cover. Ordinary people gain a free test; insurers absorb a modest new mandate.
A new no-cost-sharing benefit expands the population getting PSA tests and follow-up care, increasing demand for screening labs and urologists.
